So, she went to a dance and left the boy to stay with his grandma.” I think they were staying with her. “Let her go,” Grandma told the boy when the wife left. She didn’t take much of her things. The old woman sat in front of the fireplace and put all she had down. And there, the boy saw she had laid out some arrowheads. She had hung what they call a moccasin––you know the kind made out of deer skin––she hung it in front of where she had the arrowheads. Later on, she left and one of the arrowheads made a sound, so she went to where the bundle was on the chimney. Later on, when she came back, she said to the flint, “You didn’t do anything.” So then she sent another arrowhead and again when it came back it hadn’t done anything. “You didn’t go do anything either,” she said to it. Then she put it away. When the third one left and came back she had a container this [gestures] size with water, and the arrowhead went into it. It was washed, and the arrowhead had blood on it. “You really did something,” she said to it, then she put it up. Later on, someone came and told the boy that his wife had died at the dance. The flint must have shot her.
She was really bad, wasn’t she?

english_text: Another one? Let's see… because there’s a lot of things I know. Also, the Ukten that they talk about, have you all heard of it? One time she said they went fishing. Standing Rock, as they call it, by Oklahoma Station, near where the river is. Standing Rock, as they called it, because Grandma said a rock used to stand there. It’s underwater. These days the water isn’t as deep as she was saying around that area. There, a tree that had fallen was there. Grandma would sit on it before others started coming to fish there in the deep end. Long dresses, they wore back then. Her dress was in the way of her fishing. After a while something was moving below, she saw it and looked. It looked like a cow. It was looking at her from below. It was kind of like a greenish color, she said. Its eyes were like a cow, and its nose too, and it had horns. She watched it, she thought, “What am I going to do?” The others fishing there, she didn’t want to yell at them. “Let’s get down for a little while,” she told them, walking away. “Let’s get down for a while”. They all started walking back. They didn’t ask why when they were told to get off. When they went up a little further, she told them, and that’s when they started running, she said. That was Ukten, she used to say. That’s where it lives, she used to say, in the deep end of the water, there near Standing Rock. I think there are still some things that are living in the deep end of the water.
Amazing things they knew then.

english_text: Well how I see it, it is going to be difficult for us. Because it’s coming as the older ones predicted already. Also, they say we are going to lose our language, and I believe that is going to happen. And someday the money we are using will not be of any use for us —that’s what the older ones said too. And the gardening —if you don’t know how nothing will grow (famine will happen), even if you don’t know how to hunt, or make a garden. This Walmart that we have today—when Covid-19 happened it was hard on everybody, especially those that don’t know how to cook. McDonald’s wasn’t open, cause some people that’s all they know, they don’t know how to cook. They would go get something to eat and they are the ones that it will be hardest for. They don’t know how to grow things; they just go get something. Also, like the deer— something that’s provided for us, something will happen, so we won’t be able to eat them anymore. So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

english_text: I worked at a few different places when I was a young man. I started working at Cookson Store for a while. George Stratton was the name of the owner. His wife's name was Helen, they were good people, very friendly. I worked there for a while and then that big water came and they closed it, then they started building on the water. Boat docks they called them, for boats, and then someone from Ft. Smith came and started building some like that there at Cookson Bend was the name there. He found out I was working, and he came to Cookson, “I will pay you more if you help me build those boat docks,” he told me. “We will see what happens, I help my friend out here,” I told him. “We will talk about it. I can't go with you right away. If I can give him a week or two weeks' notice that I am going to quit, then I will go,” I told him and he agreed so that is what I did and went to build where they put boats, boat docks. He had a little store, and I worked there and then I worked there for about two years and that store owner at Cookson, his son, a young man, he was building all the way around that lake you would call it. “Did you build those building at the lake?” he said. “Yeah, I helped,” I told him. “I am not building on the water I am building on the mountain,” he told me. “I want you to help me,” he said. “This really is my house where I walk and work,” I told him. “Don’t think anything. No mistake, I can meet here at the store and leave from here in the mornings. We will go around building. A meeting place will be at Cookson,” he said. “I will give him a week notice to find someone else to help him, I can't just quit,” I told him. So, I went and helped him for a week at a time, sometimes for longer. I was building around there on the water and then when we finished all those houses around the lake there is just a few buildings we did not build. And when we finished there, St. Claire Lime Company, Sallisaw then they called me and said you can help us. I have never made white dust before.“ You will not be making any, you can just watch the workers. If they are doing good or not, you will be sitting up high. There are stairs, you can sit up high on the second step, you can show them what to do,” he told me. “I don’t know if I can show them what to do, I have never done that before. I have never made lime before,” I told them. We are going to tell you what to do, you just have to watch the meters and when you watch the meters there were several of them and when you watch the meters, they got to hold at a certain degree. All 24 hours, they can't go up, they can't go down, they got to stay right there. “I can do that,” I told him. “I know you can do it,” that boss told me. Then I started there and worked for a long time. I was working there when I went into the Army, when I got out and finished the Army, where did I start then?

english_text: I learned a lot from my dad about raising and killing hogs. And skinning them. That’s who I learned from. He turned it all over to me y’know, to gut it. He turned it all over to me. english_text: Well, we had made plans to get married. “Let’s go to the revival!" she told me. It’s at the Indian Baptist Church. So, I went with her, it was on a Thursday night. Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

english_text: Yeah, I learned it. When was it? When we lived behind the school. One time, I wasn’t there. Anyway, when I got there, “Hey, you have to go down the hill to another building to take a test. If you don’t pass it, you won’t get your certificate," they told me. So, the lady that worked with me, we went down there. “Me, I’m going to go there, but I can’t pass it, because I didn’t know how to read and write.” Because I really didn’t know back then. Anyway, I got there and I told the other woman, “I’m just gonna sit here and wait for you.” – Anyway, “I’m going to pray,” I said. “I’m going to pray real hard,” I told her. So, I prayed and asked God to help me. I told Him, “I don’t know how to read and write.” I prayed for about ten minutes. There was nothing written in front of the paper we were to fill out with syllabary. “If you don’t fill it out, then you won’t pass,” they said. I went and sat down, and the Lord just put everything in front of me. I wrote out the whole syllabary chart. I did this for the next page. I had to read it. You had to write it in English, and also the syllabary, about pages worth. The last page I had to read. Anyway, I just felt funny sitting there writing and I had to read it. “Alright. Thank you, Lord,” I said. I turned in the test paper. Then they called me in. “You did well,” she said. I looked at her, it was Bobbie Smith and Ana [Sixkiller]. They were the ones giving the test. I got 95%. I said, “Oh my gosh! Thank you, Lord!” I said. “What happened to the other 5%?” I asked her. “You went over ten minutes reading it,” she told me. I read it, but I didn’t really know how. That’s when it started, me reading well. I was really glad. If you really believe, the Lord will help you if you ask Him.

english_text: Just right over in the other hollow—Cloud Hollow. Where the church is, up that hollow. Down that way, I was born. We moved around in that area when I was growing up. The last time we moved it was straight from where the church is at the end of the hollow is. Still there—that is where we lived. And when we moved from there “Let's move for good from here,” our dad said. “We are going to travel.” We came across. Grandfather lived across by the hollow little ridge. We came there. And then, “We are moving from this hollow”, he told him. “Why? You all have been living around here a long time.” he said. “That is true. It has to be. I am going to get closer to my work.” And then we came up through the hollow. Dropping things. We came over. Then we went back into another hollow. And, where we came out, there was a little house, close. It was just this wide [gestures]. “We can live there until the summer,” he said. And water and food—there is a creek. “You all can fish there or catch crawdads. And in the evening we will eat good.” We would go there. Norman would follow us all the time. Second— in the family we were half brothers, that one. My dad was his dad, that one. His mom lived nearby. But they moved when we got there. So he stayed with us. He would be with us when we would go to the water. We would go catch lots of fish. We would eat fast, in the evening. He had a sawmill, that boss. My dad worked there. And we would go to the water every day. And then, about two years we lived there, their sawmill broke down. “I guess that’s all for us,” they said. “I guess we will go back, then.” ‘Loaded up and came back up the hollow. We came back down, close to Grandfather’s house. We came back again. [Grandfather said] “That house is still there—where you all lived.” “We are headed back to it,” he said. So, we went back over there. Then they said “Let's make a church on the hill.” They said, “There, before Anigvluyo.” It was flat. And that was our church. We would walk that far. And went there on Sunday or Saturday. At night we would be coming back. And come back there [to the original house]. It was closer for us to go, when we moved there. Then they talked about making a church right there on the hill. “On the ridge,” they said. Then they started cutting wood up, the adults. And was dragging limbs around, clearing for the workers. We made it. My dad’s brother had a sawmill there. He started milling. He milled all that, where that little building is. We made a church there. We went in there. Jen was an old lady then, she would walk using her cane. She would come up. It was like this, there. She would come in on Sunday morning.
How old was she then?

english_text: “I really think she was older than that,” I told my brother. “From what I heard, she was 114, they say,” he told me. There is a young man that lives right there. We talked the other day. “Have you seen that old lady they talk about?” he said to me. “Who, Jenny?” I said that. “How old she was ?” he told me. Then I went to Jay ‘couple days, and looked. Me and that young man that lives right there. He said: ”’Jenny Birdchopper--’ was written,” he said, “’--birthday 144 years old.’” “I believe it,” I told him. “I think it is true,” I told him. When she died, I was over there, we were talking. She had some flowers planted—just right there. She was fixing and cleaning them. ‘ She w at them. “I guess you all can do it now,” she told them. “But for now I am going in the house and rest,” she told them. I thought she was saying ‘just for now.’ “I am going to rest for now. You all stand here.” She went into the house. I was standing there, looking at them [the flowers]. And then my playmate came. “What are you looking at?” He said. “Jen was talking to those flowers she has planted there,” I told him. “All the time. Every day.” “But I am going into the house and rest,” she told them. I said to him, “She must have got tired.” “Let's go over to the water. There is two buckets, over there, we will get,” he told me. english_text: One time, this is myself—over there, where we lived. That good house, it was a ranch. We lived there. Mel was little, just little, about yea tall [gestures]. ‘Just now walking good, or she was walking good. The other was bigger. Corene, me, and Arch were adults. We were sitting there. And dad used to hunt all the time. At night time he would be listening, to the dogs he had, that chased coyotes and foxes. He would be listening—Arch and him. They were sitting there, it was dark. “I am going to the woods tonight,” I told him. “Are you going to look for possums?” “I might bring some when I am coming back,” I told him. “OK, watch yourself.” “OK, I will be carrying a light.” I told him. “Ok. ‘Dogs are tied up right there. Take them. They are old, they will not take you very far away.” He told me. I kept walking and came on up. I was walking on a ridge over there. About halfway, where I said, there was a crossroad. About there, I stopped, and the dogs scattered out. They barked way over there. So, I thought “I will just sit right here, at this tree.” There were some places to sit, so I sat down. I was sitting there, listening. When they came up they went that way. They got quite far that way. They might have found a coyote, I thought. I am going to get closer, I thought. And I got up, and I started walking. Somewhere on top I stopped, and I sat down. I was sitting there and the light started getting low. I ran out of coal oil. It got dark. “I guess I am just going to sit here. I have a fire,” I thought. “I am just going to sit here.” They were chasing just over there. They went by, and came back. I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. I stuck it on [my clothes] and then another—they started coming out. I was catching them, putting them on my clothes, and then it was kind of light. Then I started walking. I followed the road. english_text: There was just five of us. My aunt had about 20 kids. She said, “The Bible says go replenish the earth.” I think it was at Cherry Tree, Jerry Nofire said, his wife said, “Yeah, but it didn’t tell you just to do it by yourself.” And his wife was sitting there, and they had about eight or nine kids themselves. Bull is his son. He was a third-generation preacher at Cherry Tree. But Jerry started getting sick all the time, and we knew he was going to pass soon. He said, “Y’all be thinking about who’s going to be preaching for y’all,” sometime around a year before he passed. I was talking to Bull about how he should be the one [who preaches for us], and he said, “I’ve been asking for that for a long time.” We were talking and I chose Bull, and I said, “If you agree to do so, it would be you.” He said, “Let me think about it.” And then he said, “Yeah I will, because we’re going to lose that old man before too long.” And it wasn’t about a year before he really started to get sick and going in and out of the hospital. One time he came back from the hospital, and he got on to us there at church, he said, “You guys here, you’re always praying for me to get better, it’s your fault I’m still here. I’m actually ready to leave.” He was ready to leave, it was because of us praying for him, we were trying to hang on to him. He was ready to leave, that was how he was seeing it, because his wife had already left. “Well, I can’t do anything, I have to pray for you, because that’s what you’ve been teaching us,” is what I told him. We were doing what he told us to do, but he still didn’t like it because he was wanting to go home. One day he went in, they gave up on him, there wasn’t any need for them to know, and he did go home, and then people began to gather at his house. It was like buzzards when they see something laying there. They were eating, and the old man was still hanging in there. We went to visit him, I was doing something at the church, and there was a little girl that came running over to us, she said, “Somebody wants to talk to you,” and I said, “Hang on a minute, let me finish up.” She said, “He’s sitting right there,” and when I went out, there he was after they had given up on him. We talked for a long time, and I said, “What happened?” and he said, “I didn’t feel like going home, so I just thought I better get up.” He was driving that thing that runs by itself, wheelchair. He came to the church, and he said, “I guess they ate everything up, they gave up and went home.” He lasted for about a week after that, and then we were starting to figure it out, that it was close. I visited him every day until the evening, and then one evening I left, I told him I’d come back tomorrow, but first I had to go to town, and it was about 10pm when I got back, and then the phone rang, and he had left.
Yeah, your friend left.

english_text: Yeah, me too. I'm right there. If I help someone, like you said, they will want to pay. I will say, “Help the next person, because someone is going to need help.” Because I have had a lot of help in my lifetime and I just want to give some back, yep. There was an incident one time in Baldwin Wisconsin, when I was still living in Wisconsin. Me and a co-worker were driving, he was a machine operator. He had his seat pulled back. It was about 4:30 in the morning in Baldwin, going towards St. Croix Falls. No houses till like 12 or 15 miles, now there are houses everywhere. We were driving through nothing but cornfields. The corn was this high [gesture]. Out of the east came a car, and it sped up. Out of the west came another. I seen it. We were a way yet. I seen the signal light. It was going to turn where we were coming. Boy, it was coming from the east fast. He sped up his car. I said, “Gaw dernit, Rick! They are going to hit!” Rick heard me and said, “Who’s going to hit?” Soon as he did that, it was early in the morning, dark, no yard lights. All we had was lights on the cars. It just got dark. When they hit, it just turned all the lights out. A girl got killed that morning, so I parked the car on the side of the road and turned on the emergency lights. We ran over there. I went to help the one on this side, the one that got hit, and Rick went to help the one that done it. That girl, you could see that’s how she was laying down. When they hit, she went like this [gesture]. You could see her face that big on the windshield. She hit her head and broke her back. She was killed right there, and the other he was helping was like this [gesture] under the steering wheel. The gear shift was stuck right here. Not through the skull just through the skin it came out here [gesture]. I was trying to open the door so I could help them, but nothing. So I went around. It was pushed against the guard rail, and I could not get in over there. So, I ran back around this way and took my shirt off and wrapped it – I was going to break the window behind them. When I did this, someone said try this door. I had already tried that door. I was going to break the window out. I said, “I done did.” I thought Rick was standing there, and there was nobody else except me, Rick, and them people. So I said, “I done did.” He said, “Try again.” He had been hit right there [gesture]. He was just smashed. The man was in there, moaning. He said, “Tell him you are going to be with him in a minute.” I said, “Hold on, sir, I’m trying to get in to you. Just hold on,” I told him. I grabbed the door, and I done tried this door. The door opened like it was new. And this is God’s honest truth. He knows what I seen. He said, “Get in. He is badly hurt.” He told me to just lean over the seat, but he was talking in English. So I did what he said and followed it. When I grabbed that man, immediately all of my arm turned bloody. I told him what I was going to do. He said, “No, when you bring him back to the seat,” he said, “hold his head. He is really injured. Keep talking to him. Help is already coming.” Who called them? There was nobody. Cars didn’t even go by. So I stayed like that in the back. The blood was going like this here on my hands [gesture], talking to him. I did what the guy asked me to do. I did all of that. Then I seen state patrols. Two of them came. Before that, I seen what the man looked like. He didn’t have a face, and the car was hiding everything of him, but he did not have a face. I seen him. I told him OK. He was wearing red, a red and black shirt. I even put it in the state patrol statement as a witness. I wrote it all down, what I seen. So I told the state patrol. “How long ago did you do this training?” he said. I told him I ain't never done nothing like this. “How did you know what to do?” he said. I said, “That guy out there.” I grabbed him and said, “That guy out there told me what to do.” He said, “What guy?” I said, “There is a guy.” I told him what he had on. They both shined their spotlights and looked around. Nobody was anywhere around. So I said, “Rick, where did that guy go?” I said to him. He said, “What guy, Billy?” I said, “That guy that was just here.” He said, “There ain't no guy, Billy. It’s just us.” By God, he did not have a face. That is what that man told me. Out there, what I did for that man, I talked to him, I told him I wasn’t leaving him. The ambulance came. I was holding him all that time. He said, “Don’t let him go, this man, don’t let him go.” I crawled over the seat and held this man. I crawled over the seat with the ambulance people and they did that to him here. About eight months later, I was sitting at Fall Creek. I had just got back from work. My little girl – the phone rang, and I said, “Don’t answer it.” I was hungry. She quickly answered it. She said, “Hold on. Dad, it’s for you.” Man, I almost cussed. I got to the phone and said hello. They said, “Hello, is this Billy Pettit?” I said, “It’s Billy Pettit.” This is what happened: they said, “About eight months back, I was in a car accident.” Gah-lee, that’s what they said. I was back in that place. I quickly seen that man again. Y’know, there’s a smart—smartass talk… Y’know, he said, “You saved my life.” I almost said, “Did I kill a poop-eating dog?” I almost told him that, but I held my tongue. I said, “Oh, did I? How did I do this?” He said, “I was in a bad car accident. My neck was broke in three places. One bad move and I would have died underneath that steering wheel. You saved my life,” he said. Then I told him what all took place. He said, “Well, I want you to...” He told me his address. He said, “You are our family.” I didn’t even know the man. He said, “I want you to come and bring your family,” he said. “Let’s be as one.” That’s what happened – his neck was broke in three places. What that man said, he already knew how bad he was injured, and today he is still alive and well. Yeah, that’s what I am amazed with. Or I am not amazed. He didn’t have a face. I could not see his face. It was blank, but I seen everything else: his hair was brown, about this long [gesture]. I could see that because I wasn’t parked that far from it. They never found anyone. You can read my statement. I wrote everything I seen that morning.

english_text: It was pretty good back then. Based on what I know that I say it was good back then. People were important to one another, enjoyed [one] another, had humorous conversations. But, as time went on, I began to see it change. The value of things made it hard for us—on the price of things, about money. But as far as the mind and the way of thinking, it was better than the value of anything. But, nowadays, the price of things is really hard on us. The reason is people have moved from the way that they believed. And how man should walk here on this earth, with his own strength, and gather good to prosper. The way I see it, their own eyes have blinded them, Charlie. That’s what I see. As well as belief—they don’t believe anymore. They have nothing to do with the way we did things in the past. As far as I know, it is going to go back to that. Two different things are going to happen. I tell people, “It’s just going to be the way we are living now.” And, the other thing, is it going to be the way it was? And the way a person wants to be, and wants to live, he will choose. It will be good, or it will be sad. And it is sad, like I am saying, the things that are happening in the world is blinding the people. They are drawn to that. And the Lord that we have been provided is very joyful they are letting go of that. They feel like there is no truth. Quickly, they will think something else. That was the way it was. We were fishing, this One sitting here, I believe you know, too? But I don’t know if he knows where this is at? Do you know where Hickory Hollow is? Where the cemetery is? ‘Hickory Van Hollow’ they call it. Where the cemetery is, on the edge of the field, on this side, is where we used to live. In 1960 we had a drought. Charlie, where I am saying, I traveled that far through this field to the big Sallisaw Creek. A man named Man Hitter owned those fields. I would go across there with two buckets. There was a well there, on the creek. But in the creek there was no water—it was dry. That’s what happened. Then I done as much as could do, bending about to bring them water before it got hot. That’s the way it was when I grew up. And they washed... Back then washers did not exist. They call them ‘washing machine’ in English, they didn’t exist then. That far in the hollow, we were coming from there. They had one of those big things you put water in. They would take it that far to the big creek. I was telling this One, we are the same age, there is a rock there that has a groove in it. A hard rock there. I saw Mom for the first time, doing this. I was watching her I said, “Mom why are you beating those rocks? You are going to put holes in there.” I told her—we probably had one change of clothes. There was a rock there this big, ’kinda round. We were putting water in there for her, and she would put them [clothes] in there. And for soap—she was using that hard soap, all that. And, when she got enough, she pound them with the rocks. That’s when I thought she was going to put holes in our clothes. And, then we would help wring them out, just there on the creek, we hung clothes on the branches. While the clothes were drying we would look for our food. Crawdads, fish, and we would stick our hands under rocks. Yeah, we would just cook right there. Sometimes they would have potatoes. About this time there would be a garden, things like that, as well as onion. They would have a pan in the fire. They would boil crawdads in there. They would fry those crawdads. When they would get done, and when they were almost done, they would put the potatoes and onions, and those ‘kian’ they call them. Them elders always had those kian, hot peppers. They would cut those up. That was a good soup to drink. And crawdads fried real soft. Yeah that’s the way it was. And then, late in the evening, almost sundown, we would pack our clothes back to wear all the way back. That is the way it was back then. And, nowadays, they have washers and driers. I know they would, still won’t, feel like doing it [the laundry]—that’s the way it is. In the winter, we would cut wood to build a fire.

Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. We ate from them. There was a smokehouse behind this building I’m talking about. Suud used all wood when he built it. And, where he built that smokehouse to keep meat, just there on the side, was a spring. A spring there. They had built a fence that had pickets of wood. That area—they put those ducks in there, and chickens—he had built there, made of wood, years ago. A place to put hay—it was over this way to the north, was that building. Betty Christie is her name, she lives by the railroad crossing where we call ‘Bunch.’ There was a store there, at the time her dad had that store. And, on the other side, was another man. There they made cornmeal. The people that raised corn, like I said—horse pulled wagons. They would haul them in. They would have cornmeal made there. I forget how much when he would grind it... Maybe he would get five pounds for hisself? That’s the way it was. If you had something I needed, and if I had something and you needed it, they would just give each other—that that’s the way it was. It wasn’t about money, this. I know, if people would do that—like I said, it’s going to go back to that, and it’s going to go back to that—they could still have good lives. He would bring it to you, and if you had something to give, you would give him something as he was going home. That’s the way this was. It was really good.

We would all be up there, we would have those sticks—tsuyoni, with leaves. Chasing the flies off all day. Sometimes someone would get off, and someone else would get up there.
